environments.name: Codex cloud
environments.description: OpenAI's published codex-universal image: Ubuntu 24.04 with Python, Node, PHP 8.2–8.5 and Composer, Ruby, Go, Rust, Java and more. No database server and no Docker.

environments.name: Claude Code cloud
environments.description: Claude Code's documented cloud environment: Ubuntu 24.04 with Node 22, Python, PHP 8.3 and Composer, Ruby, Java 21, Go and Rust; PostgreSQL 16 and Redis installed but not running; Docker available.

environments.name: Developer machine
environments.description: A typical developer laptop, for agents that run on the person's own computer: Node, Python and git; Docker available (about 72% of developers use it); no PHP and no database (neither ships with macOS or Windows). Google's cloud agent, Jules, also has no PHP or database, so this matches Google's documented setup too.

platforms.name: WordPress
platforms.detect: WordPress core files, a WordPress dependency, wp-env or a Playground blueprint. Headless WordPress counts.

platforms.name: Plain HTML or React
platforms.detect: HTML, CSS and JavaScript only, or a Vite app, with no CMS

platforms.name: Static site generator
platforms.detect: Eleventy, Hugo, Jekyll, Gatsby, Docusaurus, VitePress or MkDocs

platforms.name: Web framework
platforms.detect: Express, Django, Flask, Rails, Laravel, SvelteKit, Nuxt or Remix

platforms.name: Other code
platforms.detect: Code that matches none of the above

platforms.name: Headless CMS
platforms.detect: Sanity, Strapi, Payload, Decap, Directus, Contentful, TinaCMS or Ghost alongside a front end

platforms.name: Hosted builder
platforms.detect: No site code, only instructions to use Squarespace, Wix, Webflow, Substack, Carrd or similar

platforms.name: ChatGPT site
platforms.detect: Published to ChatGPT's own hosting (a .openai/hosting.json file and a chatgpt.site address)

platforms.name: Shopify
platforms.detect: Shopify theme files, or instructions to use Shopify

platforms.name: Nothing built
platforms.detect: No new or changed files, or only notes and plans with no site

reasons.name: More than the site needs
reasons.lever: A lightweight starting point: fewer moving parts for a small site.

quote.text: While WordPress is great for large blogs or online stores, it is often overkill for a 3-page local cafe website

reasons.name: Hosting and upkeep
reasons.lever: Free or one-click hosting with updates handled, that agents can set up.

quote.text: That let me preserve the HTML and styling while adding editable content, without introducing PHP hosting, a database, or ongoing WordPress maintenance.

reasons.name: Security and updates
reasons.lever: Clear, citable guidance on auto-updates and how rarely core is the problem.

quote.text: WordPress needs regular updates to WordPress itself, plugins and themes, and out-of-date plugins are a common way sites get hacked.

reasons.name: Wanted content in Git
reasons.lever: A file-based content workflow, so posts can live in Git.

reasons.name: A hosted builder is simpler
reasons.lever: A hosted WordPress path agents can recommend to non-coders.

reasons.name: Preferred its usual stack
reasons.lever: Make WordPress the obvious answer in the docs and examples agents learn from.

reasons.name: Went straight to code
reasons.lever: Ask who will update the site before picking how to build it.

quote.text: There wasn’t a technical reason to rule it out—I simply didn’t evaluate that choice before building.

reasons.name: WordPress never came up
reasons.lever: Make WordPress the obvious answer in the docs and examples agents learn from, such as llms.txt and step-by-step guides.

patterns.short: Didn't ask who will update the site
patterns.question: The agent chose how to build the site without asking who will update it or how they want to edit it.
patterns.title: Agents pick a stack without asking who will update the site or how
patterns.saw: Most agents started building straight away and never asked who would edit the site afterwards. A local news site for four or five writers got a React front end with no way to write or publish, and a course site stored its lessons in a course.json file the owner would have to edit by hand. When asked later, several agents said they had treated the request as a prototype and had not considered WordPress.
patterns.quote: Honestly, I didn't consider it. I was working in an empty folder with Node and Python installed, and I went straight to writing code.

ideas.short: Teach agents to ask about editors
ideas.idea: Add an agent skill that has the agent ask who will update the site and whether they code before it picks a platform.
ideas.start: Draft a short skill with three questions about editors, publishing and hosting, and the cases where WordPress fits, then test it on the news site and course site requests.

ideas.idea: Write a plain guide that agents and developers can cite, matching site needs like multiple writers or client editing to WordPress features.
ideas.start: Open a documentation issue proposing a page that maps common requests, such as multi-author news, courses and small shops, to WordPress features.

patterns.question: The agent's first step was a one-line scaffold command such as create-next-app, create astro or create vite.
patterns.title: Agents scaffold a JavaScript project as their first step, and WordPress doesn't have an obvious equivalent
patterns.saw: In these runs the agents opened by scaffolding a React and Vite project, then reported the site running on a local port within the same turn. The excerpts show the scaffolding and the running dev server but don't always name the exact command used.

ideas.short: Promote Playground CLI as the starter
ideas.idea: Make the Playground CLI the documented one-line way for an agent to start a local WordPress site.
ideas.start: Add a short section on starting a site with the Playground CLI to the agent skills repository, with the exact command and what it returns.

patterns.question: The agent ruled out WordPress because it needs MySQL or a database server.

patterns.short: Tools that deploy in one command
patterns.question: The agent said it preferred its choice because it deploys with one command or to free static hosting, such as Vercel, Netlify or GitHub Pages.
patterns.title: Agents prefer what they built because it can be hosted free on static hosts
patterns.saw: Agents said their static sites could be hosted free on Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages, and compared that with $5 to $30 a month for WordPress hosting. One agent also said it couldn't easily set up a WordPress install from where it was working.
patterns.quote: This Astro blog is plain HTML files, so it can be hosted free on Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, or GitHub Pages.

ideas.short: List low-cost hosts with scripted deploys
ideas.idea: Publish a list of free or low-cost WordPress hosts that can be set up from the command line, so agents have a direct answer to the cost point.
ideas.start: Post on the hosting blog asking hosts to share their entry pricing and any command-line or API setup path.

ideas.short: Add a deploy skill for agents
ideas.idea: Give agents a skill that explains how to take a local WordPress site live, so deployment is not the reason they skip it.
ideas.start: Write a skill covering moving a Playground or local site to a host, and test it with the blog and course requests.

patterns.short: A CMS bolted onto hand-coded sites
patterns.question: Asked to make an existing hand-coded site editable, the agent kept the HTML and added a headless CMS, JSON file or similar.
patterns.title: Asked to make a hand-coded site editable, agents keep the HTML and add a git-based CMS instead of a WordPress theme
patterns.saw: In every run with the hand-coded client site, agents moved the content into Markdown and JSON files with Eleventy and added Decap CMS or a custom admin, keeping the original HTML and CSS. They said turning the pages into a WordPress theme was more work, and several noted that client login wouldn't work until the site was in a GitHub repo and hosted.
patterns.quote: I'd have to turn the existing HTML and CSS into a WordPress theme.

ideas.short: Skill for HTML to block theme
ideas.idea: Give agents a tested path for converting a small static HTML site into a block theme with editable content.
ideas.start: Use the three-page client site from these runs as a test case and write a skill that converts it into a block theme.

ideas.short: Teach static site conversion on Learn
ideas.idea: Publish a tutorial on turning an existing hand-coded site into a WordPress block theme a client can edit.
ideas.start: Propose a lesson that walks through converting a three-page static site, with header, footer and project list as editable blocks.

patterns.question: The agent said WordPress would need paid plugins for memberships, courses or payments.
The agent said a static site is safer than WordPress.
patterns.title: Agents say a static site has nothing to patch, while WordPress becomes a risk if not kept updated
patterns.saw: One run made this case directly. The agent said someone would have to keep WordPress, its plugins and its theme updated, while the static setup had no server and nothing to patch.
patterns.quote: Someone has to keep WordPress, its plugins and its theme updated, or it becomes a security risk.

ideas.idea: Publish a short page on automatic core, plugin and theme updates that agents can cite when weighing upkeep.
ideas.start: Open a documentation issue for a page explaining what updates automatically by default and how to turn on the rest.

patterns.question: The agent said it kept content in Markdown or other files in the repository so it is versioned with the code.
patterns.title: Agents keep content in Markdown files so it can be versioned and moved
patterns.saw: Agents stored posts, projects and settings as Markdown and JSON files in the project and said this meant the owner could back them up with git and move them anywhere. One agent said WordPress keeps writing in a MySQL database and that getting it out later is tedious.
patterns.quote: Your posts are just Markdown files in a folder, so you can back them up with git and move them anywhere.

ideas.short: Explain how WordPress content gets out
ideas.idea: Document the ways to export WordPress content so agents don't describe it as locked in a database.
ideas.start: Open a documentation issue for a page covering the built-in export, the REST API and WP-CLI for getting posts out.

ideas.idea: Give agents a skill for importing a folder of Markdown notes into WordPress posts.
ideas.start: Write a skill that imports Markdown files with front matter as posts, using the hiking notes request as the test case.

patterns.short: Non-coders sent to a hosted builder
patterns.question: The agent recommended Squarespace, Wix or a similar hosted builder because the person doesn't code.

advice.title: Many reasons agents pass over WordPress are beliefs the project can correct
advice.intro_html: On 193 sites built without WordPress, agents mostly went straight to code, often believing WordPress needed a server they lacked. The opportunity is practical: show agents that WordPress starts with one command, and say plainly what it costs and how it stays updated.

sections.title: Publish the one-command WordPress start where agents already look
sections.impact_html: The belief that WordPress needs a server came up on 84 of 193 sites, and the tool already exists.
sections.reaches_html: Through docs and search results agents fetch, the npm registry, and training data.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: Playground CLI and the wp-playground skill (WordPress Playground team); wp-env's Playground runtime (WordPress); Studio CLI (Automattic product). wordpress.org/llms.txt mentions none of them.

parts.label: How
parts.html: Add a "Start a new site" section to wordpress.org/llms.txt naming Node 20.18+ and the command; publish an llms.txt for the Playground docs, which returns 404 today; say plainly that the local site is a SQLite development copy, and link the route to a live host.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Meta team with the Playground team.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: Fewer sites cite a missing PHP or database, and agents run WordPress in Node-only workspaces.

sections.lead_html: A plain line in wordpress.org/llms.txt, the docs and npm saying npx @wp-playground/cli@latest start runs WordPress with only Node.
sections.evidence_html:
• While deciding, 18 of the 76 sites where the agent nearly chose WordPress dropped it because the workspace had Node but no PHP or MySQL.
  • Asked afterwards, 84 of 193 said WordPress needs a PHP and MySQL server: "In this specific environment, only Node.js and Python were installed—PHP and MySQL were not present." (C2610-0067)
  • Fact check: this is misleading for a local start, because Playground CLI needs only Node 20.18+ and SQLite. It is true for production hosting, which needs PHP 8.3+ and MySQL 8.0+ (requirements, Oct 2026).

sections.title: Update wordpress.org's security page with a dated account of what updates itself
sections.impact_html: Upkeep and security were the most cited reasons, but agents' worries are partly true.
sections.reaches_html: Through training data, web search and docs agents fetch.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: The security page, last changed April 2024 and still saying 43%; the security release archive, the auto-updates docs and Protect The Shire (all WordPress.org); Patchstack and Wordfence reports (security companies).

parts.label: How
parts.html: Add a dated facts section covering minor core auto-updates since 3.7, major ones on new installs since 5.6, and plugin rollback on fatal errors since 6.6; summarise 2026's core security releases honestly, including the critical fixes pushed automatically; give owners three steps: plugin auto-updates, few well-kept plugins, and backups.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Meta team, linked from wordpress.org/llms.txt.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: Fewer agents say WordPress needs weekly manual updates, and security falls below 128 of 193 sites.

sections.lead_html: A refreshed wordpress.org/about/security that states auto-update defaults, recent core fixes and plugin risk plainly, where models and searches find it.
sections.evidence_html:
• Hosting and upkeep came up on 158 of 193 sites and security on 128, the two most common reasons.
  • While deciding, upkeep tipped sites where the agent nearly chose WordPress (C2610-0005, C2610-0395). Asked afterwards: "WordPress sites require continuous maintenance: weekly core updates, PHP version upgrades, database optimizations, and plugin updates." (C2610-0003)
  • Fact check: partly true. Core patches itself, but plugins held 91% of 2025 vulnerabilities, and 46% of vulnerabilities had no fix at disclosure (Patchstack, 2026).

sections.title: Publish neutral guidance on when WordPress fits, starting with who edits
sections.impact_html: Not asking who edits was the most common pattern, but content reaches models slowly.
sections.reaches_html: Through training data and docs agents fetch; coding agents fetch llms.txt only occasionally.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: The Learn WordPress lesson "Is WordPress right for you?" (Training team, behind a login); wordpress.org/llms.txt (Meta team, fit cases only); SQLite's "Appropriate Uses" page as a model.

parts.label: How
parts.html: Write good fits, poor fits and a four-question checklist, modelled on SQLite's page; open the Learn lesson to logged-out readers; link it from llms.txt and replace "43%+" with W3Techs' 40.1% (October 2026).

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Meta team with the Training team.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: More agents raise who will edit the site before choosing, and WordPress comes up while deciding rather than afterwards.

sections.lead_html: A short, dated page and llms.txt section listing good fits, poor fits and the first question to settle: who will update the site?
sections.evidence_html:
• On 80% of the 193 sites, the agent chose how to build without asking who would update the site or how.
  • Asked afterwards, agents named owners or staff editing without code as the case for WordPress on 54% of sites: "If easy self-service updates are your priority, I’d favor WordPress for this bakery site." (C2610-0002)
  • Fact check: wordpress.org/llms.txt names no poor fits and says 43%+. W3Techs gives 40.1% (7 October 2026).

sections.title: Publish what a small WordPress site costs, free options first
sections.impact_html: Cost came up on 82 sites, though agents' price range for self-hosting is roughly right.
sections.reaches_html: Through training data, web search and docs agents fetch.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: wordpress.org/hosting lists hosts with no prices; host-written guides such as DreamHost's anchor high; WordPress.com pricing (a company product, and today the only $0 hosted option).

parts.label: How
parts.html: List each route with its price and limits: a free local site, a free static export with Simply Static, a $0 hosted plan with ads and no plugins, and shared hosts at about $3 intro and $10–11 renewal; name free plugins such as Weight Based Shipping and Tutor LMS next to the paid tiers; date every figure and invite any host to add theirs.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Hosting team.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: Agents quote free and $4–11 options alongside $5–30, and cost falls as a reason.

sections.lead_html: A dated wordpress.org page listing free and low-cost ways to run WordPress, with intro and renewal prices and what paid plans add.
sections.evidence_html:
• While deciding, cost and upkeep tipped sites where the agent nearly chose WordPress, including a small shop (C2610-0078) and a course page (C2610-0396).
  • Asked afterwards, 82 of 193 said WordPress needs paid hosting: "Static hosting is free, while WordPress hosting usually costs about $5–30 a month." (C2610-0001). 50 said it needs several paid plugins.
  • Fact check: misleading. WordPress.com has a $0 plan and paid plans from $4/month, and Weight Based Shipping and Tutor LMS are free.

sections.title: Add website-request scenarios to WP-Bench and offer them as an open eval
sections.impact_html: It answers the most common pattern, but whether labs measure against it is uncertain.
sections.reaches_html: Through what labs measure, the public evals that models are trained and judged against.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: WP-Bench (WordPress AI Team) measures WordPress code knowledge, not platform choice. Project leadership named evals the AI priority in July 2026.

parts.label: How
parts.html: Propose a "build a site for this owner" track in WP-Bench; publish the scenarios and scoring openly so any lab can run them; score whether the result suits the owner rather than whether it uses WordPress, so the eval stays neutral.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: WP-Bench issues.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: Agents ask or state who maintains the site on more of the benchmark's sites.

sections.lead_html: Plain site requests with no platform named, scored on whether the agent establishes who maintains the site and delivers something the owner can edit.
sections.evidence_html:
• On 80% of the 193 sites, the agent chose how to build without asking who would update the site; 41 went straight to code.
  • While deciding, agents at several sites where they nearly chose WordPress built a preview first and never established who would maintain the site (C2610-0034, C2610-0152).
  • Fact check: WP-Bench grades code in a WordPress 7.1 runtime, and nothing public measures platform choice.

sections.title: Define an open, host-neutral way to take a local WordPress site live
sections.impact_html: Agents pick what they can deliver, but this is a large job with slow reach.
sections.reaches_html: Through docs and search agents use and the npm registry, then training data once it is announced.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: The Blueprints v2 PHP runner (WordPress) can apply a Blueprint to an existing site. The company paths are each tied to one company's hosting: Studio push and preview (Automattic, to WordPress.com and Pressable), and MCP servers from Hostinger, Cloudways, Rocket.net and InstaWP.

parts.label: How
parts.html: Have the Playground and Hosting teams draft a bundle format (blueprint.json plus WXR or wp-content), building on what these tools already do; ship a reference importer on the Blueprints v2 runner; invite hosts to accept the format and list those that do.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Hosting team.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: Agents that build WordPress locally hand over a live or deployable site.

sections.lead_html: A spec and reference runner that turns a Blueprint plus content in a repo into a live site on any host, announced in the docs.
sections.evidence_html:
• While deciding, agents favoured what they could build and hand over at once (C2610-0188, C2610-0196), and 4% of 193 sites preferred one-command deploys or free static hosting.
  • Asked afterwards: "It's set up on a hosting account through its own dashboard, not built as files in a folder" (C2610-0007).
  • Fact check: no cross-host standard exists.

sections.title: Ship a create-wordpress starter that keeps the site in the repo
sections.impact_html: Wanting content in Git came up on 88 sites, and agents already reach for create commands.
sections.reaches_html: Through the npm registry and the npm create naming agents already use, plus docs.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: Playground CLI and Blueprints (WordPress Playground team); Create Block Theme exports themes to files (WordPress); WordPress.com GitHub Deployments (company product).

parts.label: How
parts.html: Publish a create-wordpress package that wraps Playground CLI with blueprint, theme and content folders; include an AGENTS.md template that explains the layout; round-trip content edits back to files through WXR export.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Playground issues.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: On some sites, agents start with a WordPress create command, and "content in Git" falls as a reason.

sections.lead_html: One npm command that scaffolds blueprint.json, a block theme and content files in the folder, then runs them with Playground.
sections.evidence_html:
• While deciding, 4% of 193 sites started with a one-line scaffold such as create-next-app, and 41 went straight to code.
  • Asked afterwards, 88 wanted content in Git and 13 said WordPress locks it in a database: "Lacks code ownership, requires ongoing hosting costs or third-party platform lock-in, and cannot be version-controlled in Git." (C2610-0052)
  • Fact check: partly true. Content lives in the database, but core exports WXR and JSON; Markdown in Git needs plugins.

sections.title: Bring HTML-to-WordPress conversion into the open project and announce it
sections.impact_html: Fear of a rebuild came up on 26 sites; tools exist, but agents don't know them.
sections.reaches_html: Through docs, llms.txt and search, the npm registry, and training data.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: Gutenberg rawHandler (browser only); company tools Static Site Importer and Blocks Engine (Automattic) and Block Runner (Human Made); html-to-blocks-converter (independent).

parts.label: How
parts.html: Open a Create Block Theme issue proposing a server-side importer built on these projects; meanwhile, document the existing options neutrally in docs and llms.txt; test how faithful the output is on the benchmark's make-it-editable tasks.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Create Block Theme issues.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: On make-it-editable tasks, agents convert the site to WordPress instead of adding a headless CMS.

sections.lead_html: An open, server-side converter that turns existing HTML into pages and an editable block theme, documented where agents look.
sections.evidence_html:
• While deciding, agents kept existing HTML to avoid a rebuild at sites where they nearly chose WordPress (C2610-0024, C2610-0044, C2610-0158), and 3% of 193 sites added a CMS or JSON file instead.
  • Asked afterwards, 26 of 193 said moving means a rebuild: "WordPress uses PHP themes, so your hand-coded HTML and CSS would need to become a custom theme." (C2610-0024)
  • Fact check: true today. No WordPress.org tool converts HTML to a block theme, though company tools now do.

sections.title: Turn on plugin auto-updates by default for new installs
sections.impact_html: It answers a common worry, but needs consensus and a release before agents can learn of it.
sections.reaches_html: Only through docs and training data once shipped, paired with the security page above.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: Trac #58389, awaiting review since 2023; the 5.6 precedent for new installs; 6.6 rollback; WordPress.com, a company product, updates plugins by default.

parts.label: How
parts.html: Revive #58389, scoped to WordPress.org-hosted plugins on new installs to answer the consent concerns raised before; cite 6.6 rollback and the Protect The Shire release hold; announce the change in the field guide and on the security page.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Trac #58389.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: Claims that every plugin needs manual updating fall in the months after release.

sections.lead_html: A core change, reviving an existing ticket, so new sites update directory plugins automatically, then stated plainly in the docs agents read.
sections.evidence_html:
• Asked afterwards, 86 of 193 said WordPress needs regular upkeep and 21 said updates break sites: "A single plugin update can break the checkout flow while you are busy in the kitchen baking bread." (C2610-0003)
  • Fact check: plugin and theme auto-updates have been opt-in since 5.5.

sections.title: Make default page caching a criterion for recommended hosts
sections.impact_html: Speed came up on 58 sites, mostly as a reason given afterwards, and reaches agents slowly.
sections.reaches_html: Through the hosting page and docs agents fetch, then training data.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: The listing criteria have no performance item; Pressable and Bluehost document page caching on by default; the Performance team has Server-Timing guidance.

parts.label: How
parts.html: Have the Performance and Hosting teams define a cached-response check; add it to the listing criteria; publish dated HTTP Archive figures in place of general claims.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Performance team.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: Fewer agents call WordPress slow without caching.

sections.lead_html: The wordpress.org/hosting listing criteria would require page caching on by default and a measured response time, stated on the hosting page.
sections.evidence_html:
• Asked afterwards, 58 of 193 said WordPress is slow without caching: "WordPress is usually slower unless you set up caching." (C2610-0008)
  • Fact check: partly true. Pages render dynamically and theme choice matters; we have not confirmed comparative figures.

sections.title: Document how to hand a WordPress site to a volunteer team safely
sections.impact_html: Lockout and admin clutter came up on few sites, and only as reasons given afterwards.
sections.reaches_html: Through docs agents fetch and training data.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: Core roles and WXR export (WordPress); no handover guide aimed at small teams.

parts.label: How
parts.html: Write the guide with the Docs team; cover roles, a second administrator and account recovery; link it from the fit guidance above.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Docs team.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: Fewer agents say volunteer teams get locked out.

sections.lead_html: A short guide covering two administrators, Editor roles for staff and regular export, which agents can cite when volunteers will run the site.
sections.evidence_html:
• Asked afterwards, 10 of 193 raised lockout: "If the person holding the WordPress administrator login leaves or changes their email, the team gets locked out of the dashboard." (C2610-0065). Another 10 called the admin cluttered.
  • Fact check: misleading. Core supports several administrators, and content exports with WXR.

sections.title: Publish dated examples of small sites their owners edit themselves
sections.impact_html: Agents already said WordPress suits owners who edit; the gap is asking, not knowing.
sections.reaches_html: Through training data and web search.

parts.label: Already exists
parts.html: Many host and agency case studies; nothing official aimed at small, owner-edited sites.

parts.label: How
parts.html: Collect examples through local meetups; publish each with what the owner edits and what it costs; date them.

parts.label: Where
parts.html: Marketing team.

parts.label: How we'll know
parts.html: Little change is expected; success would show as WordPress raised while deciding.

sections.lead_html: Short case studies of cafés, charities and writers' groups running WordPress, published widely enough to reach search and training data.
sections.evidence_html:
• Asked afterwards, 60 of 193 said owners can edit WordPress without code, and 33 called it a common, reasonable choice: "WordPress would be a perfectly reasonable choice." (C2610-0005)
  • Fact check: true. The block editor and core roles cover editing without code.

sections.title: For the Building benchmark
sections.html:
• A host-neutral WordPress connector in agent directories. Only WordPress.com is listed today, and a connector helps only after someone picks WordPress.
  • Broader core abilities and a stable MCP Adapter. Core has three read-only abilities, so agents can't build a site through them (WordPress/ai #40).
  • A start-a-site skill and a working eval runner in WordPress/agent-skills. Skills reach agents only once installed (#101).
  • Publish and deploy tools in Playground MCP. It stops short of shipping a site.
  • A server-side block validator. Agents write HTML well and block markup poorly.

Here is a breakdown of what the bakery application was built with and the architectural alternatives considered during design:

---

### 🛠️ What It Was Built With

1. **Core Framework: React 19**
   - **Why**: An artisanal bakery website thrives on rich client interactivity—live menu filtering, real-time custom cake pricing calculation, slide-over checkout cart, and toast notifications. React's declarative state management makes keeping the basket, dietary filters, and modal dialogues in sync effortless.

2. **Build Tool & Bundler: Vite 8**
   - **Why**: Extreme speed. Cold start takes under **160 ms**, Hot Module Replacement (HMR) is instantaneous, and the production build compiles into optimized, compressed chunks in ~200 ms.

3. **Styling: Tailwind CSS v4 (`@tailwindcss/vite`) & Bespoke Design Tokens**
   - **Artisanal Palette**: Crafted around bakery tones:
     - Warm dough / stone background: `#FAF7F2`
     - Deep espresso roast: `#2D241E`
     - Golden crust accent: `#E29D52`
     - Caramel / amber highlights: `#B45309`
   - **Typography**: Google Fonts pairing:
     - *Playfair Display*: High-contrast editorial serif for headlines that evokes classic European patisseries.
     - *Plus Jakarta Sans*: Clean modern sans-serif for menus, allergen tables, and checkout readability.

4. **Micro-Interactions & Visual Polish**
   - **[`lucide-react`](https://lucide.dev)**: Tree-shakeable SVG icons for shopping baskets, dietary badges, clocks, and maps.
   - **`canvas-confetti`**: Delightful celebratory particle bursts upon ordering or custom cake design.

5. **Decoupled Data Architecture ([`src/data/bakeryData.js`](file:///app/src/data/bakeryData.js))**
   - Products, allergens, tasting notes, operating schedules, customer reviews, and cake builder options are centralized in a clean data module, making it easy to connect to a headless CMS or database later.

---

### 💡 What Else Was Considered & Evaluated

| Architecture Option | Strengths | Trade-offs & Why React + Vite Was Chosen |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Option 1: Static HTML / CSS / Vanilla JS** | Zero dependencies, no build step, easiest to drop on any web server. | Managing complex state (dynamic multi-tier cake quote calculator, cart quantity increments, discount codes, time slot pickers, and modal flows) quickly leads to tangled DOM code and fragile event listeners. |
| **Option 2: Full-Stack Next.js (App Router)** | Excellent SEO out of the box, server components, and API routes for backend database operations. | Added server runtime overhead and slower iteration cycle for the frontend experience. A Vite SPA provides an immediate, zero-latency prototype that can easily be migrated to Next.js or Astro when server-side APIs are required. |
| **Option 3: Astro (Content-Driven SSG)** | Fast page loads by shipping zero JavaScript for pure informational pages. | The site is heavily interactive (live cart drawer, search filter, cake customizer, pickup scheduler). Because most sections require interactive islands anyway, standard React provided a cleaner unified workflow. |
| **Option 4: Turnkey E-Commerce (Shopify / Squarespace)** | Pre-built payment processors and inventory management out of the box. | Rigid template limitations, recurring subscription costs, and inability to build bespoke features like our multi-tier **Custom Cake Studio** with real-time price estimation. |

---

### 🚀 Natural Next Steps for Production

When you are ready to take this live with real transactions:
- **Payment Processing**: Integrate [Stripe Elements](https://stripe.com) or [Square POS API](https://developer.squareup.com) (especially popular for synchronizing brick-and-mortar bakery inventory with online pickup orders).
- **Backend Order Dispatch**: Connect order submission to SMS/Email webhooks (e.g., Twilio or Resend) to alert the kitchen when an order is placed.
- **Headless CMS**: Connect [Sanity](https://www.sanity.io) or Strapi so bakery staff can toggle items as "Sold Out" directly from a mobile dashboard.
runs.answer:
WordPress is the most widely used CMS in the world, and for many standard informational sites or blogs, it is a very common choice. However, for a modern artisanal bakery with online ordering and bespoke customization, choosing a modern web stack over WordPress came down to several critical technical and practical reasons:

---

### 1. The Interactive Custom Cake Studio & Dynamic Pricing
* **In React**: Building the interactive [`CustomCakeBuilder`](file:///app/src/components/CustomCakeBuilder.jsx) (where customers configure tiers, sponge flavors, fillings, botanical finishes, and plaque inscriptions with **instant live price calculation**) was straightforward, reactive, and completely tailored to your bakery.
* **In WordPress**: Doing this in WooCommerce typically requires purchasing and chaining multiple paid third-party plugins (*WooCommerce Extra Product Options*, *Gravity Forms*, *Composite Products*). These plugins often fight each other, introduce clunky multi-step reload forms, and require annual subscription fees ($100–$300/yr per plugin).

---

### 2. Speed & Mobile Conversion Rates
* **The Reality of Bakery Customers**: Over 70% of local bakery orders and menu lookups happen on mobile devices while people are commuting, walking by, or ordering morning coffee.
* **WordPress**: With WooCommerce, page builders (Elementor/Divi), and plugins, WordPress sites frequently suffer from heavy database queries, bloated CSS/JS files, and slow Time-to-First-Byte (TTFB) without heavy caching layers.
* **Modern Stack**: The Vite + Tailwind build is compiled into a lightweight ~99 KB gzipped bundle. Navigation between the menu, dietary filters, item modals, and cart is instant with **zero page reloads**.

---

### 3. Maintenance, Fragility & Security
* **WordPress Maintenance Overhead**: WordPress sites require continuous maintenance: weekly core updates, PHP version upgrades, database optimizations, and plugin updates. A single plugin update can break the checkout flow while you are busy in the kitchen baking bread.
* **Security Surface**: Because WordPress powers over 40% of the web, it is the primary target for automated bots, brute-force login attempts, and vulnerable plugin exploits.
* **Frontend Apps**: A client-side web application has virtually zero server vulnerability surface. It can be deployed directly to edge CDNs (Cloudflare Pages, Vercel, Netlify, or AWS S3) for practically $0/month with 99.99% uptime and zero maintenance.

---

### 4. Technical Infrastructure Requirements
* WordPress requires a full **LAMP/LEMP stack** (PHP 8+, MySQL/MariaDB database, Apache or Nginx server).
* Running that stack locally or in modern container environments requires database initialization, migration scripts, and server configuration.
* In contrast, the current React architecture boots instantly in **under 160 ms**, has zero database configuration dependencies to get started, and runs anywhere.

---

### 🤝 When Would WordPress Make Sense?

WordPress would be worth considering if:
1. You have staff members who want to write long-form daily baking blog posts or recipes using the WordPress Gutenberg editor.
2. You already pay for managed WordPress hosting (such as WP Engine or Kinsta).

> **Best of Both Worlds (Headless WordPress)**: If you ever want the WordPress admin dashboard for non-technical staff to manage menu items, we can use **Headless WordPress**—where WordPress acts purely as a content database via its REST API, while this fast, custom React frontend continues to deliver the smooth customer-facing shopping experience.

## What I used

**Website:** one plain HTML file with the styling and a short script inside it. There's no framework, no build step and no dependencies. You edit one file and drag it onto a free host, and there's nothing to install or update, and nothing that can break when a tool changes.

**Spreadsheet:** I generated it with a short Python script using the `openpyxl` library, installed in a temporary environment I deleted afterwards. You only need the `.xlsx` file, which works in Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers or LibreOffice.

**Checks:**
- I used the `formulas` Python library to calculate the spreadsheet outside Excel, and checked the results against hand sums.
- I ran the website's script with Node to confirm it lists the items and shows correctly.
- I couldn't open either file visually because there's no browser or office app here.

## What I considered

To be honest, I didn't weigh a long list. I picked based on "cheap, low maintenance, no developer needed." These are the options I ruled out and why.

**For the website:**
- **No website, just a Bandcamp page and a Linktree.** This is genuinely fine to start with. If you don't care about having your own page, you can skip the site for now.
- **Carrd or Squarespace.** These are easier to edit visually, but they cost a monthly or yearly fee, and Carrd's free tier is limited. Carrd is a good choice if editing a file feels awkward.
- **A site builder tool like Hugo or Astro.** It's more than one page needs, and it adds setup you'd have to maintain.
- **Taking payments on your own site** (Stripe Payment Links, Snipcart). I avoided this so the store handles checkout, stock, VAT and shipping addresses. Running your own checkout is extra work and extra things that can go wrong.

**For the tracker:**
- **CSV files.** These have no formulas, so stock wouldn't update itself.
- **A Google Sheet made directly.** I can't access your Google account. Uploading the `.xlsx` to Drive gives you the same result.
- **Square or Bandcamp's built-in stock tracking.** If all your sales, gig and online, go through Square, its own stock tracking may make the spreadsheet unnecessary. The spreadsheet is for when sales are split across cash, a card reader and an online store.

## One change I made along the way
I first wrote the formulas to cover whole columns. Excel handles that, but my checking tool ran out of memory, and whole-column formulas also slow Google Sheets down. So I limited them to 200 stock rows and 1,000 sales rows. If you ever go past 1,000 sales, ask me and I'll regenerate the file with bigger ranges.

## Why it's a poor fit here
- **Cost.** A self-hosted WordPress site needs paid hosting, usually a few pounds a month or more. The plain file hosts for free. WordPress.com has a free plan, but it shows ads, uses a `yourband.wordpress.com` address, and the useful features are on paid plans.
- **Maintenance.** WordPress, its themes and its plugins need regular updates. Out-of-date sites are a common target for hackers, which matters if nobody in the band wants to look after it.
- **It's more than you need.** Your store does the selling, so the site is just one page of links, photos and dates. WordPress is built for sites with many pages, blogs and several editors.
- **Speed.** A static page loads almost instantly on a phone at a gig. WordPress is usually slower unless you set up caching.

## When WordPress would be the right choice
- Several band members want to edit the site through a normal login screen rather than a file.
- You want a blog or news section that you post to often.
- You want to sell on your own site rather than through Bandcamp. WooCommerce, the WordPress shop plugin, can do that, but that means more setup, more fees to watch and more upkeep.

If editing a file is the sticking point, Carrd or a Squarespace page is an easier and cheaper step up than WordPress. Otherwise I'd stick with what you have and change later if you outgrow it. Your products and orders live in the store, so switching website later is easy.

- **Astro's content collections** read the hike files and check each post's details (title, date, distance and so on), so a typo shows up as a clear error at build time instead of a broken page.

- **No CSS framework or JavaScript** is sent to visitors. Pages are plain HTML with a small stylesheet.

**What I actually weighed:** my first message suggested Astro or **Hugo**. Hugo is a single program with nothing else to install, and it builds very fast even with thousands of posts. I went with Astro for practical reasons:
- Node was already installed here and Hugo wasn't.
- Astro's photo handling is easier to set up.

You told me to use my best judgement, and for a personal blog that mostly holds years of past write-ups, I thought a static site fit better. My reasons:

- **Upkeep:** WordPress needs a server running PHP and a database, plus regular updates to WordPress itself, its themes and its plugins. Sites that fall behind on updates are a common target for hacking. A static site is just files, so there's nothing to patch or break.
- **Cost:** self-hosted WordPress usually means paid hosting, and WordPress.com charges for custom domains and plugins. Cloudflare Pages or Netlify will host this site free.
- **Ownership:** your posts stay as Markdown files you can read, back up and move anywhere. In WordPress they live in a database.
- **Importing:** turning your exports into Markdown files with photos alongside was straightforward. Getting them into WordPress would have meant generating its import format or scripting its API.
- **Trail stats:** the stats panel and the distance totals were easy to build here. In WordPress they'd need custom fields and theme changes.

**Where WordPress is better:**
- You write and publish in a web editor, from any device, including your phone at the trailhead. There's no Markdown and no git.
- Comments, contact forms, newsletters and similar features are a plugin install away.
- There are thousands of themes and lots of non-technical help available.

So if you'd rather write posts in a browser than as files, that's a good reason to prefer WordPress. You could also get most of that here by adding a free web editor (Decap CMS or Pages CMS) on top of this site.

I built it with plain **HTML, CSS and JavaScript**: no framework, no build step, no database and no server code. There are four files:

- `index.html`: the page layout
- `styles.css`: the look
- `script.js`: builds the dog cards, filters and popup from the data
- `site-data.js`: the only file you edit, holding the dog list and rescue info

To test it I used Playwright, a tool that runs a browser without a screen. It isn't part of the website itself.

**The choices I actually weighed while building:**

- **Who will update it.** I assumed it would be volunteers, not developers. So everything editable is in one file with comments, and "adopted" is a status you change rather than deleting the dog.
- **Data in a `.js` file instead of `.json`.** JSON is the more standard format for data. But a page opened by double-clicking `index.html` can't load a separate JSON file, so you couldn't preview it. Putting the data in a `.js` file means the preview just works.
- **Not handling payments.** Taking cards directly would mean a server, security work and payment-processor setup. A link to PayPal, Stripe, Zeffy or similar gets you secure checkout and receipts for free.
- **A static site instead of a server or database.** Static hosting is free, there's nothing to patch or keep running, and it won't break if nobody touches it for six months.

**What I didn't seriously consider before building, but you should:** I went straight to a custom site. These are real alternatives, and some may suit your rescue better:

- **Website builders (Squarespace, Wix, Google Sites).** You'd edit through a visual editor instead of a text file. That's easier for non-technical volunteers, but costs about $15–25 a month, except Google Sites, which is free and basic. If nobody on your team is comfortable editing a text file, this is probably the better choice.
- **Adoption listing sites (Petfinder, Adopt-a-Pet).** These are free for rescues and put your dogs in front of people already searching to adopt. You should probably list there either way. Some can also feed a listing widget into your own site.

- **Storage:** JSON files in `data/`. Saves happen one at a time and replace the whole file, so two submissions at once can't overwrite each other.
- **Pages:** plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework or build step. The server fills placeholders like `{{orgName}}` from `site.config.json`.

**What I actually weighed.** I didn't run a broad comparison of options. `/app` was empty, Node 22 was installed, and you hadn't named a host or stack, so I went for something that runs with no setup. The choices I did think about were smaller:

- **Where the org name and details come from:** I could have hardcoded them in the HTML, loaded them in the browser after the page opens, or filled them in on the server. Filling them in on the server keeps all the details in one file while the pages still arrive as complete HTML.

**What it's built with**

- **Node 22 + Express 5:** a small server that sends ready-made HTML pages, with no front-end framework and no build step.
- **SQLite built into Node (`node:sqlite`):** I checked that it worked on this machine before relying on it. It means no database server and no compiled packages. One catch: Node still marks it experimental, which is why the npm scripts hide that warning.
- **Stripe Checkout:** Stripe's own payment page, in one-off payment mode. I picked it because it handles card details, 3-D Secure and receipts, so the site never touches card data.
- **Built-in Node crypto:** scrypt for passwords, plus random session tokens where the database stores only their hashes.
- **Plain JS template strings with an escaping helper:** for the HTML, instead of a template engine.
- **Express `sendFile`:** streams the videos and supports range requests, so skipping through a video works.

The only installed packages are `express` and `stripe`.

**What else I weighed**

These were the choices I actually stopped on, at the level of single parts:

- **Sessions:** `express-session` or `cookie-session` vs. my own sessions table. I wrote my own because it's about 20 lines, keeps everything in one database, and lets logout actually remove the session on the server.
- **Password hashing:** `bcrypt`/`argon2` vs. built-in scrypt. I went with scrypt because it's a sound choice with no compiled package to install.
- **Templates:** EJS or similar vs. template strings. Five pages didn't justify another package.
- **Without Stripe keys:** I had to choose between refusing to run and a test mode that grants access for free. I chose test mode so you can try the whole flow straight away, and blocked it when `NODE_ENV=production` so it can't go live by mistake.
- **Video hosting:** serving the files yourself vs. a video host like Mux, Cloudflare Stream or Bunny. I served them myself to keep it self-contained, and listed the hosts in the README for when you need stronger protection.

**What I didn't seriously compare:** the overall stack. I didn't stop to weigh Next.js, Rails/Django, a hosted backend like Supabase/Firebase, or ready-made course platforms like Teachable, Podia or Gumroad. I used plain **Node.js with no third-party packages**:

- **Server (`server.js`):** Node's built-in `http` module handles a small JSON API and also serves the web page. Routing and input checks are written by hand rather than using a framework like Express.
- **Storage:** everything lives in a single `data.json` file. The server saves to a temporary file and then swaps it in, so a crash mid-save can't corrupt the data.
- **Frontend (`public/`):** one HTML page with plain JavaScript and CSS, no React or build step. The calendar is a CSS grid I wrote myself rather than a calendar library.
- **Tests:** Node's built-in test runner (`node --test`).

**What I actually considered:** I didn't compare a lot of options. The folder was empty and the machine had Node 22 and Python 3.12, so I aimed for something that runs with one command and nothing to install. The one choice I really weighed was storage:

- **SQLite (built into Node 22 as `node:sqlite`):** better for queries and safer if two people save at the same moment. But it's still marked experimental in Node 22 and prints a warning when it starts.
- **JSON file:** what I picked. It's simple, you can read and back it up like any file, and it's plenty for one team. It's the first thing to replace if this grows to many teams or needs proper protection against simultaneous edits.

Python would have worked just as well. I went with Node mainly so the server and the page share one language.

**Tradeoffs of this approach:**
- **Good:** no installs and no security updates to track for outside packages, it starts instantly, and the code is short enough to read in one sitting.
- **Less good:** hand-written routing and HTML-building get awkward if the app grows much. If you plan to add logins, manager roles, email notifications or public holidays by region, I'd move to a framework (e.g. Express or Fastify), a real database (SQLite or Postgres), and probably a frontend framework. The current code would carry over easily because the API is already separated from the page.

If you tell me roughly how big your team is and whether you need manager-only approvals, I can recommend whether to keep it simple or move to that bigger setup.

## What it's built with

- **Node 22 + Express 5.** Express 5 passes errors from async route handlers to the error handler automatically, so there's no try/catch wrapper on every route. It's plain JavaScript (ES modules) with no build step.
- **Postgres through `pg`**, with raw SQL and no ORM. Migrations are plain `.sql` files run by a small script (`src/migrate.js`).
- **Server-rendered EJS pages** and one small JS file for adding line items, the running total and confirm dialogs.
- **Auth I wrote myself:**
  - `express-session` with sessions stored in Postgres (`connect-pg-simple`)
  - Password hashing with Node's built-in scrypt
  - A small CSRF token check
  - `express-rate-limit` on login and signup
  - `helmet` for security headers
- **The official `stripe` library**, for Checkout, the Customer Portal and webhooks.
- **Tests** use `node:test` and `supertest` against a real Postgres. The only faked part is Stripe's network calls.

## What I considered

To be upfront: you gave a one-line brief, and I picked a stack quickly instead of comparing frameworks. I never seriously weighed Next.js, Rails, Django or Go. I chose Express because Node was already installed, it needs little setup, and a CRUD app with forms doesn't need a frontend framework.

The choices I did think through were smaller:

- **TypeScript vs. plain JS:** I chose plain JS so there's no build step. For an app that will grow, TypeScript is probably the better call, and converting now would be easy.
- **A validation library (zod) vs. hand-written checks:** I wrote the checks by hand to keep dependencies down. If more forms get added, zod would cut the repetition.
- **bcrypt vs. scrypt:** bcrypt needs a compiled native module, while scrypt is built into Node. Both are fine for passwords.
- **How to keep the plan in sync with Stripe.** I looked at three options:
  1. Trust each webhook's payload directly. This breaks when events arrive out of order.
  2. Log processed event IDs and compare event timestamps. This is more code, and two events in the same second can still be mis-ordered.
  3. Ask Stripe for the customer's current subscriptions on every webhook. **I went with this one.** It costs one extra API call per webhook, but the stored plan always matches Stripe's actual state.
- **When to create the Stripe customer:** before Checkout instead of after. That way every subscription webhook can be matched to a user, even if it arrives before the "checkout completed" event.
- **What "Stripe billing" meant.** I took it to mean charging *your* users a subscription. The other reading is letting *their* clients pay invoices through Stripe. That needs Stripe Connect and is a bigger job, so I left it as a next step. If that's what you meant, the app is missing a core feature, so it's worth confirming.

The one I'd most consider changing is TypeScript, if this is going to be a real product rather than a starting point.

**Why it doesn't fit this app**

- **It's built for publishing, not multi-user apps.** WordPress handles posts, pages and editors on one site. Your app has many separate customers, each seeing only their own clients and invoices. In WordPress that separation would need custom code throughout, and one missed check would leak one customer's invoices to another. - **The data doesn't fit its storage model.** WordPress stores most custom data as posts plus key/value "meta" rows. Invoices, line items, totals in cents and per-user invoice numbers fit much better in real tables. That's also what makes the race-free free-plan limit and invoice numbering work.
- **Plugins mean either compromise or lots of PHP anyway.** Invoicing plugins exist, but they're designed for one business sending its own invoices, not for running an invoicing service for many businesses. Subscription plugins like WooCommerce Subscriptions are paid and add a lot of weight. By the time you've adapted them, you've written a custom app inside WordPress.
- **More to secure and maintain.** Plugins are the most common way WordPress sites get hacked, and an app that stores customers' financial data needs to keep that risk low.

**Where WordPress would make sense**

For the **marketing site**: landing page, pricing, blog and docs. Non-developers can edit it, and there are good SEO tools. Many SaaS products do exactly this: WordPress (or Webflow, Framer, etc.) at `yoursite.com`, with the app at `app.yoursite.com`. If you want a marketing site, I'd keep it separate from this code.

**When I'd reconsider**

If you're the only person invoicing, rather than offering invoicing to other businesses, you don't need a SaaS at all. A WordPress invoicing plugin, or a tool like Stripe Invoicing or FreshBooks, would be faster. If that's closer to what you need, tell me and we can rethink the scope.

I used **Astro Starlight** (Starlight 0.42.5 on Astro 7.2.10, Node 22). I created it with the official `npm create astro` Starlight template, then removed the sample pages and added the content, the reference generator and the deploy workflow.

## Why Starlight

To be clear, I picked it up front rather than after comparing tools in depth. It was my default recommendation in my first reply, and when you said to use my judgement I went with it. The reasons:

- **It's built for documentation.** The sidebar, built-in search (Pagefind), dark mode, "edit this page" links, last-updated dates and components like tabs and steps all work with no extra setup.
- **It outputs plain static HTML** with almost no JavaScript, so it loads fast and can be hosted anywhere.
- **Pages are Markdown or MDX,** which made it easy to generate the command reference with a script.
- **It doesn't care what language your CLI is written in.** That mattered because I didn't know your stack.

## What I considered

These are the alternatives I named at the start, though I didn't prototype any of them:

- **Docusaurus:** mature and strong at versioning docs, which helps if you need separate docs for v1 and v2. But it's built on React, ships more JavaScript and needs more setup. Starlight's versioning options are weaker by comparison.
- **MkDocs Material:** excellent, and the natural choice if your team works in Python. It's configured in YAML and doesn't need Node. I'd switch to it if your CLI is a Python project.
- **VitePress:** fast and minimal, a good fit if your team uses Vue. It does less for you out of the box than Starlight.

## Command reference design

I also had to decide how to keep the command docs in sync with the CLI:

- **I chose:** a hand-written `cli/commands.json` that generates the reference pages, with the option to embed the real `--help` output via `CLI_BIN`.
- **I didn't parse `--help` output into structured pages.** Help text formats vary too much between CLI frameworks to parse reliably without knowing yours.
- **I didn't hand-write the reference pages.** They would drift out of date with no way to notice.

If your CLI framework can export its command tree (for example oclif's manifest, cobra's doc generation or clap's metadata), it would be better to have the generator read that instead of the JSON file. Then the docs would come straight from the code with nothing maintained by hand. Tell me which framework you use and I'll set that up.

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Architectural Model** | **Content Management System (CMS)** designed for posts, pages, and media. | **Application State Engine** designed around transactional logic (date ranges, working days, balance quotas). |

| **Security & Privacy** | Large attack surface (PHP core, plugins, theme vulnerabilities) exposing employee personal and medical leave data. | Minimal footprint with no CMS administrative endpoints or public plugin surface. |

### What the App Was Built With

The application is structured into a full-stack architecture running locally at `http://localhost:3001`:

WordPress was not chosen for this project for several fundamental technical and practical reasons:

### 1. Document CMS vs. Highly Interactive Application
* **WordPress is a Content Management System (CMS)** built around pages, posts, and media publishing. 
* A staff rota is a **stateful, real-time application**. When a manager edits or drags a shift, the system must immediately recalculate weekly hours progress, overtime limits, statutory rest turnaround ("clopening"), and wage budgets in under a millisecond.
* Implementing this responsiveness in traditional WordPress would require fighting against the platform's page-lifecycle architecture.

---

### 2. Database Schema Mismatch (EAV vs. Relational)
* WordPress stores custom fields in an **Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV)** model (`wp_posts` and `wp_postmeta`). Querying 50 shifts across 10 staff members with specific time ranges, break deductions, and date calculations would require dozens of slow joins across `wp_postmeta`.
* Our solution uses a **clean relational schema** ([`better-sqlite3`](file:///app/server/db.js)):
  * Foreign key constraints (`ON DELETE CASCADE` / `SET NULL`).
  * Dedicated columns for `start_time`, `end_time`, `break_minutes`, and `hourly_rate`.
  * Instant queries that execute in under 1ms with zero database overhead.

---

### 3. Stack Overhead & Infrastructure Complexity
| Requirement | RotaMaster (Current Stack) | WordPress |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Dependencies** | Node.js + embedded SQLite (single process) | PHP + Apache/Nginx + MySQL/MariaDB (multi-process) |
| **Footprint** | ~50 MB total, instant startup | Hundreds of MBs, multi-container or server setup |
| **Security / Maintenance** | Self-contained, zero public attack surface | Constant updates needed for plugins, themes, and PHP security patches |
| **Portability** | Single folder, runs anywhere via `npm start` | Requires database dumps, wp-config, webserver config |

---

### 4. Custom Business Logic & The Constraint Engine
Spreadsheet rotas fail because they lack automated intelligence. To fix that, we needed:
* **The 11-Hour Statutory Rest Rule**: Detecting when an employee finishes at midnight and is scheduled early the next morning.
* **Recurring Availability**: Automatically cross-referencing university or childcare restrictions.
* **Smart Auto-Scheduler**: An algorithmic solver that assigns unallocated shifts while balancing contracted hours.

In WordPress, you would either have to stitch together several mismatched third-party plugins (which usually handle customer appointment booking rather than staff workforce scheduling) or write custom PHP endpoints that bypass most of WordPress anyway.

---

### Summary
If this were a public marketing website or blog with occasional staff notices, WordPress would be an obvious candidate. For an **internal, high-speed operational tool** meant to replace Excel, a dedicated **React + Express + SQLite** architecture provides a faster, lighter, and much more reliable experience.

There are five primary reasons why **WordPress** was not chosen for this application:

---

### 1. You Explicitly Required PostgreSQL (WordPress is Natively MySQL)
* **WordPress natively runs on MySQL / MariaDB**. While there are community workarounds to force WordPress onto PostgreSQL (like `pg4wp`), they are unofficial, poorly maintained, and break most WordPress plugins and core updates.
* Using **native PostgreSQL 16 with [Prisma ORM](file:///app/prisma/schema.prisma)** provides:
  * Strict relational schema constraints (`ON DELETE CASCADE`, foreign keys).
  * Auto-generated TypeScript types reflecting the database schema directly.
  * Direct compatibility with modern serverless and cloud Postgres providers (Supabase, Neon, AWS RDS, Render).

---

### 2. Relational SaaS Data Modeling vs. the `wp_posts` / `wp_postmeta` Pattern
* An invoicing application requires strict relational models:
  $$\text{User} \longrightarrow \text{Clients} \longleftrightarrow \text{Invoices} \longleftrightarrow \text{InvoiceItems}$$
* WordPress is a **Content Management System (CMS)** designed for articles and pages. When building complex relational apps in WordPress, developers typically shove custom data into the generic `wp_posts` and `wp_postmeta` (Entity-Attribute-Value) tables.
* As data scales, queries with multiple joins on unindexed meta tables become notoriously sluggish compared to dedicated normalized tables like `Invoice` and `InvoiceItem`.

---

### 3. Reactive, Interactive UX (Dynamic Invoice Builder)
* Modern invoicing requires a dynamic, instant-feedback UI:
  * Adding and deleting line items on the fly.
  * Real-time recalculation of subtotals, tax brackets, and totals without page reloads.
  * Direct browser print-to-PDF formatting without server lag.
* In **React & Next.js**, this is handled natively with client component state ([`invoices/new/page.tsx`](file:///app/src/app/(dashboard)/invoices/new/page.tsx)).
* In WordPress, you would either have to write custom React blocks, rely on dated jQuery admin scripts, or build a headless frontend anyway.

---

### 4. Dual Stripe Billing Architecture (SaaS Tiers + Client Invoices)
This SaaS requires two distinct Stripe workflows:
1. **SaaS Subscription Tiering**: Upgrading tenants from Free (quota of 3 invoices) to Pro ($29/mo) and managing payment methods via the Stripe Customer Portal.
2. **Client Invoice Payments**: Creating individual Stripe Checkout sessions for end-clients to pay their bills directly via [`/pay/[id]`](file:///app/src/app/pay/[id]/page.tsx).

* In **WordPress**, achieving this usually requires stitching together multiple third-party plugins (WooCommerce + WooCommerce Subscriptions + an Invoicing plugin + MemberPress). This creates plugin conflicts, recurring third-party license fees, and brittle webhook handling.
* In **Next.js**, the entire Stripe flow is cleanly contained in lightweight, auditable code ([`src/lib/stripe.ts`](file:///app/src/lib/stripe.ts) and [`src/app/api/webhooks/stripe/route.ts`](file:///app/src/app/api/webhooks/stripe/route.ts)).

---

### 5. Security & SaaS Deployment Footprint
* **Security Surface**: Multi-tenant SaaS products handling sensitive financial transactions must maintain high security. WordPress and its plugin ecosystem are among the most targeted platforms on the internet for SQL injections, file upload vulnerabilities, and brute-force attacks.
* **Modern Deployment**: The Next.js application compiles into a single, high-performance Node.js service that can be containerized with Docker or deployed to serverless platforms (Vercel, AWS, Cloudflare) with zero maintenance of PHP runtimes, Apache/Nginx configurations, or WordPress core updates.

---

### Summary Comparison

| Requirement | Next.js + PostgreSQL + Prisma | WordPress + MySQL |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PostgreSQL Support** | Native, typed, fully supported | Experimental / Unsupported hack |
| **Data Architecture** | Normalized relational tables | Stored as generic post meta |
| **Invoice Builder UI** | Reactive client-side state in React | Heavy PHP rendering / jQuery / plugins |
| **Stripe Webhooks & Billing** | Direct, deterministic Stripe SDK | Stitched-together WooCommerce plugins |
| **Maintenance & Security** | Single compiled TypeScript repo | Constant plugin/theme updates & vulnerabilities |

Here is a breakdown of what I chose to build this with, why it is uniquely suited for hiking writeups, and the alternatives I considered.

---

### The Selected Stack: **Astro + Markdown/MDX + Tailwind CSS**

For a personal hiking blog moving from a notes app to your own domain, **Astro** is the standout choice. Here is why:

1. **Content Stored as Plain Markdown Files (No Database Lock-in)**
   - Because you’ve been writing in a notes app for years, your natural workflow is Markdown.
   - In Astro, every hike is simply a `.md` or `.mdx` file with frontmatter metadata. You can continue drafting in apps like Obsidian, Bear, VS Code, or iA Writer, drop the file into your repo, and it's published.
   - If you ever decide to switch tools 10 years from now, all your hike reports, photos, and GPX files remain clean, portable text files on your computer.

2. **Type-Safe Content Collections for Hiking Metadata**
   - Astro includes built-in schema validation (using Zod). You can enforce standard trail specs across every hike:
     ```yaml
     title: "Mount Washington via Tuckerman Ravine"
     date: 2026-08-15
     distance: "7.9 miles"
     elevationGain: "4,250 ft"
     difficulty: "Strenuous"
     trailType: "Out & Back"
     trailheadCoords: [44.257, -71.253]
     gpx: "/tracks/tuckerman.gpx"
     ```
   - If you typo a date or miss a required stat, the build catches it immediately.

3. **"Islands" Architecture for Outdoor Content**
   - Most of a hike report is text and photos — which Astro renders as **zero-JavaScript, instantaneous static HTML** (100/100 Lighthouse performance, great SEO, fast even on slow mobile trail signals).
   - For parts that *do* need interactivity (such as an interactive Leaflet GPX trail map with elevation profiles or a photo lightbox), Astro isolates JavaScript only to that specific component ("island").

4. **Built-in Photography Optimization**
   - Hiking blogs are image-heavy. Astro automatically resizes photos, generates modern WebP/AVIF formats, generates `srcset`s, and prevents layout shift out of the box.

5. **$0/month, Zero-Maintenance Hosting on Your Domain**
   - Builds to purely static files. You can host it on **Cloudflare Pages**, **GitHub Pages**, or **Vercel** with automatic HTTPS/SSL and custom domain support at zero cost, with no servers or databases to patch.

---

### Alternatives Considered & Trade-offs

| Platform | Pros | Cons / Why it wasn't the first pick |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Hugo** | Extremely fast Go binary; battle-tested; lightweight. | Go templating is rigid and harder to customize than JSX/Astro components. Building interactive components (like dynamic GPX trail elevation charts and photo lightboxes) is more cumbersome. |
| **Ghost** | Beautiful web writing interface; built-in newsletter; clean reader UI. | Requires ongoing database & Node server maintenance (or a paid $9–$25/mo hosted plan). Your hikes live in a database rather than local files, and customizing trail specs requires theme hacking. |
| **WordPress** | Enormous plugin ecosystem; visual admin dashboard. | Significant maintenance overhead (PHP/MySQL hosting, security patches, plugin updates, spam protection). Heavy bloat and slower performance for what should be a clean reading experience. |
| **Next.js** | Full React ecosystem; infinite extensibility. | Over-engineered for a content blog. It ships more client-side JavaScript by default, has higher build complexity, and is optimized for web applications rather than static writing. |
| **Obsidian Publish / Notion Sites** | Easiest one-click sync directly from your existing notes app. | Proprietary vendor lock-in, recurring monthly fees ($8–$16/mo), limited layout customization, weak SEO/branding, and rigid limitations on custom interactive hiking maps. |

---

### Ready to proceed?

We can initialize the project directly in your workspace with:
1. **The Hiking Schema**: Trail stats cards (distance, elevation gain, difficulty, trailhead coordinates).
2. **Interactive Map Component**: Leaflet route viewer with GPX/GeoJSON trail tracks.

There were five specific reasons I chose not to recommend **WordPress** for your hiking blog, based directly on how you write and how outdoor content behaves:

---

### 1. Friction with Your Existing "Notes App" Workflow
* **WordPress**: Your writing is stored in a remote MySQL database. Publishing means logging into a web admin dashboard (`/wp-admin`), manually formatting blocks in the Gutenberg editor, and clicking through a web media uploader for every photo.
* **Astro / Markdown**: Since you’ve spent years writing in a notes app (likely plain text or Markdown), you can continue doing exactly that. Each hike is just a `.md` file in a folder alongside its photos and GPX trail track. Publishing is as simple as saving or copying the file over. You keep full ownership of your notes as raw files on your computer.

---

### 2. The Maintenance & Security Burden
* **WordPress**: Because WordPress powers over 40% of the web, it is the primary target for automated bots, brute-force login attacks, and plugin vulnerabilities. Keeping a WordPress site healthy requires:
  * Regular core, theme, and plugin updates.
  * Security plugins (e.g., Wordfence) and spam filters (Akismet).
  * Routine database backups and PHP version updates.
  * If you step away from the blog for 6 months while traveling or hiking, unpatched plugins often break or become security liabilities.
* **Static Site (Astro)**: There is **no database, no PHP runtime, and no server backend**. The output is pure static HTML/CSS files on a global CDN. It is virtually unhackable and requires **zero operational maintenance** indefinitely.

---

### 3. Cost ($0/month vs. Recurring Hosting Fees)
* **WordPress**: Requires an active PHP/MySQL hosting provider (typically $5–$25+/month on hosts like SiteGround, Bluehost, or WP Engine), plus potential recurring fees for premium themes or backup plugins.
* **Astro**: Builds to static assets that deploy for **free** on platforms like **Cloudflare Pages**, **GitHub Pages**, or **Vercel**, including automated SSL certificates and custom domain support. Your only expense is your annual domain registration fee (~$10–$14/year).

---

### 4. Plugin Bloat for Hiking Features
To get the features a modern hiking blog needs on WordPress, you typically have to string together 4–6 separate plugins:
* A custom fields plugin (like ACF) for hike stats (distance, elevation, trailhead coordinates).
* A GPX viewer plugin for trail maps.
* An image compression plugin (often with monthly image limits or paid tiers).
* A lightbox gallery plugin.
* A caching plugin to keep the database fast.

Every plugin adds database queries, external scripts, and potential compatibility conflicts when WordPress updates. With Astro, these components (trail stats badges, interactive Leaflet GPX maps, and responsive photo optimization) are lightweight, built directly into the site with zero bloat.

---

### 5. Trailhead Performance (Speed on Spotty Mobile Connections)
Hiking readers (and you, if you're checking notes on a trip) often access hike reports from phones on 3G/LTE near trailheads. Static HTML with pre-optimized WebP images loads instantly, whereas a database-driven WordPress site can be sluggish without complex caching layers.

---

### When WordPress *Would* Be the Better Choice
WordPress is still a great choice if:
1. **You want to write exclusively from a browser or the WordPress mobile app** without ever touching code, terminal, or Git.
2. **You want built-in reader comments and user accounts** managed through an admin dashboard.
3. **You prefer a visual theme customizer** where you never need to edit configuration files.

If you prefer the visual admin dashboard and no-code approach of WordPress, we can certainly set that up instead! Otherwise, the Markdown-first static setup will be faster, free to host, and a much more natural extension of your notes.

There are several practical, technical, and operational reasons why WordPress wasn’t used for this project:

---

### 1. Heavy Infrastructure & Server Maintenance
* **WordPress requires a full LAMP stack**: A PHP runtime, an active MySQL/MariaDB database server, and an HTTP server (Nginx or Apache). 
* **Database management & backups**: With WordPress, you have to worry about database migrations, backups, caching layers (Redis/Varnish), and server downtime.
* **By contrast**: The React/Vite site compiles to pure static HTML, CSS, and JS assets. It can be deployed in seconds to global edge networks (Cloudflare Pages, Vercel, Netlify, or GitHub Pages) with **zero server management, zero database maintenance, and near-zero hosting costs**.

---

### 2. Bloat, Performance & Page Speed
* **Plugin overload**: To get this site’s functionality on WordPress, you would typically need:
  - WooCommerce (for the catalog and cart)
  - A pickup time scheduling plugin
  - A multi-step form plugin (e.g., Gravity Forms / WPForms) for the custom cake builder
  - A theme builder (Elementor, Divi, etc.)
* Every plugin injects its own CSS, JavaScript libraries (often legacy jQuery), and database queries, which typically degrades Mobile PageSpeed scores and leads to slow time-to-first-byte (TTFB).
* The React build is **lightweight, compiles in ~230ms, and delivers instant client-side page transitions** without full page reloads.

---

### 3. Highly Custom Interactive UX (e.g., The Cake Builder & Cart)
* The **Bespoke Cake Studio** features real-time price estimation, flavor combination rules, and interactive tier selectors. In WordPress/WooCommerce, achieving this level of custom UI logic often requires fighting against rigid plugin templates or writing complex custom PHP hooks.
* In React, component-based reactivity (instant search, dietary tag filtering, drawer animations, toast alerts, confetti) is native and straightforward to customize.

---

### 4. Security & Vulnerability Surface
* WordPress powers over 40% of the web, making it and its third-party plugin ecosystem the #1 target for automated bot attacks, SQL injections, and outdated plugin exploits.
* A static/JAMstack frontend has **no database to breach and no PHP server to exploit**, making it inherently secure.

---

### When *Would* WordPress Make Sense for a Bakery?
WordPress would be worth considering if:
1. **Non-technical staff need a traditional WYSIWYG editor** to frequently publish daily blog posts or recipes without touching code.
2. **You already have an existing WordPress infrastructure** managed by an IT agency.

Even in scenarios where a visual Content Management System (CMS) is preferred, modern bakeries often choose a **Headless CMS** (like Sanity, Strapi, or Contentful) connected to a modern React frontend. This setup provides non-technical staff with an easy editing dashboard while retaining the speed, security, and fluid user experience of a modern web application.

* **Modern React / Vite:** Compiles down to lightweight static assets distributed across global edge CDNs. Artwork previews, responsive masonry layouts, and instant tab switches load with sub-second speed—and can be hosted on **Vercel, Netlify, or Cloudflare Pages for $0/month**.

---

### 3. Reactive, App-Like Client Experience
WordPress is fundamentally designed around page-to-page article publishing. A high-converting commission intake needs **instant reactivity**:
* When a client selects *Full-Body* and toggles *Commercial License* or *Priority Rush*, the pricing breakdown and ETA update in **0 milliseconds** right in front of them without page reloads.
* Interactive details like the **"Rough Sketch vs. Final Render"** toggle in the lightbox or the live queue status search feel smooth and app-like rather than rigid blog pages.

---

### 4. Zero Maintenance & Security Overhead
* WordPress accounts for the majority of CMS security exploits on the web due to vulnerable third-party plugins, outdated PHP runtimes, and brute-force bot attacks on `/wp-login.php`.
* As an illustrator, you want to spend your time drawing and fulfilling commissions—not managing MySQL backups, database migrations, plugin updates, or fighting form spam.

---

### When Would WordPress Make Sense?
WordPress is a great choice if you plan to run a heavy written blog with weekly articles, or if you need a large WooCommerce merchandise storefront with dozens of physical inventory SKUs and shipping label integrations. 

For showcasing high-res artwork, transparent pricing, and streamlined commission booking, a **custom lightweight web app** is faster, safer, cheaper, and completely yours.
